description: We’re AstroNox, a team passionate about space exploration, machine learning, and software engineering. We combine AI, computer vision, and 3D visualization to solve real-world challenges. For NASA Space Apps, we’re building an interactive 3D Mars explorer to analyze terrain and help plan safer rover routes using NASA data and ML.
summary:
We built Gale Marswalk Planner, an interactive web app that turns NASA orbital maps and Curiosity rover observations into a tool for exploring Mars and planning simulated astronaut walks. Users can zoom from a global view of Mars into Gale Crater, explore 3D terrain at selected rover stops, and choose where to start and end a walk.

The planner uses slope, terrain roughness, and mapped hazards to find a route within a user-selected slope limit. It estimates walking time, energy use, and oxygen needs so users can compare routes before choosing one. In the 3D close-ups, we preserve NASA’s stereo measurements and use AI to fill gaps where depth measurements are missing.

This matters because the shortest route across Mars can cross steep or rocky ground and take more time or energy than a longer route. By bringing terrain, hazards, and resource estimates into one view, our project makes those trade-offs visible and shows how real mission data can inform future human exploration.
details:
I developed Marswalk AI, an interactive Mars terrain explorer and astronaut walk-planning prototype focused on Gale Crater and Curiosity rover locations. My goal was to make complex Martian terrain data accessible through an interactive experience that connects planetary-scale exploration with detailed, rover-level terrain analysis.

I designed the application to let users navigate through multiple levels of exploration, starting from a global view of Mars, moving into Gale Crater, exploring a detailed planning area, and finally inspecting rover stops through interactive 3D terrain reconstructions.

To build the system, I integrated NASA/JPL Curiosity Navcam imagery, stereo XYZ products, PDS camera metadata, rover traverse data, weather context, and USGS Gale Crater terrain products. I used NASA stereo geometry as the measured reference for terrain reconstruction. Where stereo depth contained missing regions, I incorporated the pretrained Depth Anything V2 Small model to estimate relative depth. I aligned these estimates with valid stereo measurements and used them only to fill missing regions rather than replace measured data.

I implemented the terrain reconstruction pipeline using CAHV camera geometry and rover pose information to generate point clouds, terrain grids, 3D meshes, slope layers, and geometrically identified rock and ledge hazards.

For route planning, I developed an A* pathfinding system operating on a 2-metre terrain grid. Users can select their starting and ending points, and the planner evaluates possible routes while avoiding missing terrain data, excessive slopes, blocked hazards, and high-cost terrain. The system provides route distance, ascent and descent, maximum slope, estimated walking time, hazard exposure, and demonstration-level energy and oxygen estimates. These estimates are intended for educational and engineering demonstrations, not as official NASA EVA rules or operational astronaut guidance.

I built the scientific processing pipeline in Python and used NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, PyTorch, and Hugging Face Transformers for the terrain and depth-estimation workflows. I developed the frontend using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Three.js and WebGL powering the interactive 3D visualization. I also incorporated FastAPI and Uvicorn for service adapters, alongside optional Rasterio, OpenCV, Plotly, and Matplotlib tooling. I used pytest and Node.js tests for testing.

One of the most important aspects of my project was designing an evidence-based, multi-scale exploration experience. I wanted users to understand not only what the terrain looks like but also where the underlying information comes from and how reliable it is. The application distinguishes between terrain measured through NASA stereo geometry and regions estimated using AI, making uncertainty and data limitations part of the experience.

Throughout development, I considered terrain uncertainty, missing stereo coverage, slope constraints, obstacle height, traversability costs, visual clarity, browser and mobile performance, and reproducibility. I also made a conscious effort not to overstate the scientific accuracy or operational capabilities of the system.

I believe the biggest contribution of Marswalk AI is its ability to connect planetary science, computer vision, artificial intelligence, 3D visualization, and pathfinding into one interactive platform. By transforming complex NASA planetary datasets into an understandable terrain exploration and route-planning experience, I hope to make Mars exploration more accessible and provide a foundation for future research into terrain-aware navigation and safer planetary exploration simulations.

The project was developed using the software and computational tools documented in the repository. I have not claimed a specific development hardware configuration because a verified hardware specification is not documented.
